title: The Afternoon Brief: Defamation verdict, federal settlements, and infrastructure strain reshape midday
dek: The midday brings a rare defamation loss for the New York Times, federal enforcement actions against TikTok and the Panama Canal reducing traffic due to drought. Internationally, Hong Kong convicts activists under its national security law, Israel reopens a West Bank settlement, and Russian drones strike a Ukrainian shopping mall.
author: GoCheckMyNews
key_fact: A jury awarded $9.25 million to a former Alabama basketball player in the Times' first defamation loss in over 50 years, exposing vulnerabilities in crime reporting; federal enforcement continues against major platforms; and critical infrastructure worldwide faces mounting strain from geopolitical conflict and climate disruption.
bottom_line: Today consolidated liability for major institutions, the Times on crime reporting, TikTok on children's privacy, Jones on Sandy Hook falsehoods, while infrastructure worldwide tightened under strain: the Panama Canal cuts traffic due to drought, the Colorado River loses 1.25 million acre-feet annually, and Ukraine faces renewed strikes. Internationally, Hong Kong's national security law reached sentencing phase on activism charges, Israel completed its reversal of the 2005 Disengagement by reopening Kadim, and California Democrats selected a Gaza-critical candidate despite organized opposition spending. Watch the September 15 Panama Canal capacity reduction, October 16 Snelling sentencing, October 19 Colorado River agreement deadline, October 26 Jeffries trial start, and whether any of the midday's federal cases advance toward trial or settlement.
body: The midday centers on three enforcement and accountability strands: courts holding major institutions liable for specific factual falsehoods, federal agencies securing settlements to enforce privacy law, and the physical infrastructure of global commerce tightening under drought and conflict.

The day's most significant verdict came from an Alabama jury awarding $9.25 million to Kai Spears, a University of Alabama walk-on basketball player, after the New York Times published a false report placing him at the scene of a fatal 2023 shooting in Tuscaloosa. The Times' 2023 article stated that surveillance video showed Spears in a car struck by bullets during the shooting; reporting established the claim was unfounded. The judgment marks the Times' first defamation loss on a published article in over 50 years, according to the desk's reporting. Separately, the Department of Justice announced a $400 million settlement with TikTok and ByteDance resolving Children's Online Privacy Protection Act litigation, with $300 million due immediately and $100 million contingent on vacating a prior consent decree against TikTok's predecessor, Musical.ly. The desk's reporting characterized the settlement as one of the largest COPPA recoveries ever obtained.

Federal courts also moved multiple high-profile cases forward. A federal judge ruled former Abercrombie & Fitch CEO Mike Jeffries competent to stand trial on sex trafficking charges, reversing an earlier incompetency finding based on claims of dementia and Alzheimer's. Judge Nusrat Choudhury based her decision on examination of medical records and over 21 hours of audio recordings across 109 calls, finding Jeffries fluent and capable of understanding proceedings. Trial is scheduled to begin October 26. In Texas, an appellate court reduced a $50 million judgment against Infowars founder Alex Jones to $1.5 million, finding Sandy Hook parents did not prove harassment rose to a level exceeding Texas's $750,000 damages cap per plaintiff; a separate $1.4 billion Connecticut judgment against Jones remains unchanged. A former University of Kentucky student-athlete, Laken Snelling, pleaded guilty to first-degree manslaughter in the death of her newborn son, whose body was found in a closet in 2024; sentencing is scheduled for October 16.

International developments widened across geopolitical and environmental fronts. The Panama Canal Authority announced it will cut daily vessel traffic from 36 to 32 ships starting September 15, citing insufficient rainfall caused by El Niño. The U.S. Department of the Interior mandated a 1.25 million acre-feet annual Colorado River water reduction for California, Nevada, and Arizona for 2027-2028, with Arizona bearing the largest cut at 760,000 acre-feet, though federal officials warned of possible additional cuts over the next decade. In Ukraine, two Russian drones struck a shopping mall in Kryvyi Rih in a double-tap attack, killing 16 people and injuring 130, with 4 still missing; the second drone targeted emergency workers responding to the first strike. Israel resettled 30 families at the Kadim settlement in the occupied West Bank, completing the reopening of all four settlements evacuated in 2005 as part of the Disengagement Plan. In Hong Kong, two activists, Lee Cheuk-yan and Chow Hang-tung, were convicted under the national security law of inciting subversion for organizing annual vigils commemorating the 1989 Tiananmen Square crackdown; a third defendant, Albert Ho, pleaded guilty in January. Both Lee and Chow face a maximum of 10 years in prison, with sentencing pending.

Domestically, the Pentagon fired Stars and Stripes publisher Max Lederer, editor-in-chief Erik Slavin, and Middle East correspondent Lara Korte on Friday, citing insubordination over unauthorized participation in a CBS Sunday Morning segment about the Pentagon's effort to overhaul the paper. Lederer's refusal to fire Slavin and Korte at Pentagon direction contributed to his own dismissal. The fired staffers were granted five days to appeal. Separately, Chief Justice John Roberts issued a temporary stay allowing President Trump's White House ballroom construction to proceed, blocking lower court rulings that would have halted the above-ground portion of the $400 million project. The National Trust for Historic Preservation had challenged the project on grounds of presidential authority and aesthetic concerns; the stay does not resolve the underlying dispute.

In California, State Sen. Aisha Wahab won the special election for the state's 14th House District with 53 percent to 47 percent against Democrat Melissa Hernandez when 95 percent of votes were counted, according to NBC News. Wahab will fill the remainder of former Rep. Eric Swalwell's term. A $2.5 million AIPAC-aligned super PAC campaign ran against Wahab, who has called Israel's conduct in Gaza genocide.

A twin-engine Cessna 441 operated by Security Aviation crashed at Cape Newenham Long Range Radar Site Airport in western Alaska on Thursday at 12:15 p.m. local time, killing all eight people aboard: two pilots and six passengers contracted by the Army Corps of Engineers. The National Transportation Safety Board is leading the investigation.
